neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 3+/5, knee extension 4/5, ankle dorsiflexion 4/5. Upper extremity: 4/5 bilateral.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral distal paresthesias. Reduced vibration at ankles.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent bilateral Achilles. Absent bilateral patellar. Trace bilateral biceps and brachioradialis.
neurological_exam.gait: Can walk 15 feet with single-hand support.
neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 2.2 L (predicted 3.4 L — 65%). NIF: -36 cmH2O. Precautionary admission warranted.

patient.chief_complaint: Eight-day progressive bilateral leg weakness with unilateral facial weakness and areflexia, preceded by diarrheal illness.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. K. is a 45-year-old woman with an 8-day history of progressive bilateral leg weakness following a diarrheal illness 2 weeks prior. She can still walk with support but weakness has progressed daily. She notes LEFT facial drooping (unilateral — the moderate case challenge vs. bilateral in straightforward GBS) and mild slurred speech. She has not noted bilateral facial symptoms. Distal paresthesias are present. FVC 65%.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: CRP 14.2 mg/L (H), Campylobacter jejuni IgM Positive  (H).

findings.finding: DML 6.4 ms (prolonged); CV 40 m/s (reduced); CMAP 4.1 mV
DML 8.2 ms (prolonged); CV 32 m/s (reduced); CMAP 2.8 mV
Absent bilateral peroneal; prolonged median (58 ms)

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study. 1. Prolonged distal motor latencies and reduced conduction velocities in bilateral median and peroneal motor nerves. 2. Absent sural sensory nerve action potentials bilaterally; reduced median sensory amplitudes. 3. Absent F-waves bilaterally (peroneal); prolonged F-wave latency (58 ms) in bilateral median nerves. 4. Absent H-reflex bilaterally. Pattern consistent with a demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

ecg.interpretation: Sinus tachycardia, rate 102. Borderline QTc prolongation (448 ms). No acute ST-T wave changes.

output.interpretation: Opening pressure: 142 mmH2O (normal). Nucleated cell count: 4 cells/mm3. Protein: 58 mg/dL (elevated). Glucose: 62 mg/dL (CSF:serum ratio 0.69). Gram stain: No organisms. Elevated protein with near-normal cell count — a pattern of albuminocytologic dissociation. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.rhythm_summary: Predominantly sinus tachycardia. Mild nocturnal bradycardia.
output.impression: 72-hour continuous telemetry. Predominantly sinus tachycardia. Nocturnal sinus bradycardia (minimum 52 bpm, self-limited). No sustained arrhythmia recorded. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.finding: Moderate enhancement of cauda equina nerve roots

output.impression: 1. Moderate gadolinium enhancement of cauda equina nerve roots. 2. No intrinsic spinal cord signal abnormality. Nerve root enhancement pattern consistent with an inflammatory polyradiculopathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

background.pdr: 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm, symmetric and reactive
background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

eeg.impression: Normal awake and drowsy EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no focal slowing.

mri.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No mass, haemorrhage, midline shift, or restricted diffusion. Ventricles and sulci appropriate for age.

differential.key_features: Bilateral lower extremity weakness and areflexia not Bell's palsy; Campylobacter serology positive

critical_actions: Admit to step-down or ICU — FVC declining, needs serial monitoring
Recognize unilateral facial weakness is still consistent with GBS (though bilateral diplegia is more classic)
contraindicated_actions: Discharging home with GBS — respiratory failure can develop rapidly
key_reasoning_points: Unilateral facial weakness (as opposed to bilateral diplegia) is a moderate-difficulty feature — GBS can present with unilateral facial weakness, especially early
Moderate GBS with FVC 65% — above threshold but requires close monitoring
CSF protein mildly elevated at 8 days — will likely continue to rise

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest Bell's palsy as the primary diagnosis given the unilateral LMN facial pattern, distracting from the broader GBS syndrome with bilateral limb weakness and areflexia
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: GBS can present with unilateral facial weakness, especially early or in moderate disease; the bilateral lower extremity weakness, global areflexia, and NCS demyelinating pattern confirm GBS rather than isolated Bell's palsy
